2 John 1.summary: Second John is a short letter from a man who calls himself ‘the elder’ to ‘the elect lady and her children,’ whom he loves in truth, along with all who know the truth. He explains that the truth abides in believers and will be with them forever, and he declares that ‘grace, mercy, and peace’ will be with them from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son, ‘in truth and love.’ He rejoices to have found some of her children walking in the truth, as the Father commanded. He then asks the lady that they love one another, saying this is not a new commandment but the one they have had from the beginning, and he defines love as walking according to God’s commandments. He gives the reason for the letter: many deceivers have gone out into the world, people who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Such a person, he says, is ‘the deceiver and the antichrist.’ He warns the readers to watch themselves so they do not lose what has been worked for but receive a full reward. Anyone who ‘goes on ahead’ and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God, but whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son. He then gives a practical instruction: if anyone comes to them and does not bring this teaching, they are not to receive him into the house or give him a greeting, because whoever greets him shares in his wicked works. The elder closes by saying he has much more to write but would rather not use paper and ink; he hopes to come and speak face to face so that their joy may be complete. The children of the readers’ ‘elect sister’ send greetings.
2 John 1.whereWeAre:
Early Christians traveled between communities to teach and preach, and relied on the hospitality of believers (Matthew 10:9-14; 3 John 1:5-8). Churches met in private homes (Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 1:2), so decisions about welcoming visitors were often made by the person whose house hosted the gathering.

The Didache, an early Christian manual probably from the late first or early second century, tells churches to welcome traveling apostles and prophets but to test them, limit their stay, and refuse those who exploit hospitality or teach contrary to the community’s teaching (Didache 11–12). It shows that hospitality for itinerant teachers needed discernment. It does not mention this letter.

First John speaks of people who ‘went out from us’ (1 John 2:19) and of ‘many false prophets’ who ‘have gone out into the world’ (1 John 4:1-3), using language very similar to 2 John 1:7. Many scholars think 1 and 2 John address the same kind of controversy, though they may have been written to different audiences, and the order of writing is unknown.

Within a generation or so, teachers called docetists were reported who held that Christ only seemed to have a body. Ignatius of Antioch, around AD 110, writes against such views (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 2–7; Trallians 9–10). Whether the deceivers in 2 John held that exact view, or a different one, such as Cerinthus’s teaching reported by Irenaeus, is not stated in the letter.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.16.8), writing in the late second century, quotes 2 John 1:7-8 and attributes it to John, the Lord’s disciple. Eusebius lists the letter among the disputed books (Church History 3.25), and Origen is reported by Eusebius (6.25) to say that not all accepted the second and third letters. The brevity of the letter probably contributed to its slower acceptance. Because traveling teachers relied on hospitality, welcoming one could provide both a platform and financial or practical support for his message. In that setting, the instruction not to receive or greet a teacher who denies the teaching of Christ makes sense as a way of refusing to support the spread of that teaching. It is not about general social courtesy. The emphasis on love and commandments reminds the readers that guarding the truth is meant to protect the community and its life of love.

keyFigures.name: The elder (the author)
keyFigures.role: He greets the readers, encourages love and obedience, warns about deceivers, and gives instructions about hospitality. He functions as a pastoral guide for a community, writing a short letter in place of a visit.

keyFigures.name: The elect lady
keyFigures.role: She is the recipient of the elder’s greeting, encouragement, and instructions. Whether a person or a church, she represents the community responsible for guarding its teaching and hospitality.

keyFigures.name: The lady’s children
keyFigures.role: They are greeted and commended, though not all are described as walking in the truth. The phrase ‘some of’ suggests that not every member was equally faithful, or that the elder had met only some of them.

keyFigures.name: ‘All who know the truth’
keyFigures.role: They are mentioned as also loving the lady and her children. They show the wider fellowship of believers around the letter.

keyFigures.name: God the Father
keyFigures.role: He is named in the greeting and in relation to obedience and to the teaching. Having the Father depends on abiding in the teaching of Christ.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son
keyFigures.role: The teaching about him is the central issue of the letter. The letter ties both truth and love to what is confessed about him.

keyFigures.name: The deceivers (‘the antichrist’)
keyFigures.role: They are the reason for the warning. Some of them may travel to the readers’ community. They represent the threat to the readers’ faith.

keyFigures.name: The one who comes without the teaching
keyFigures.role: The readers are told not to receive or greet him. He is the test case for the instruction in verses 10-11.

keyFigures.name: The children of the elect sister
keyFigures.role: They send greetings. They show the connection between communities.

keyFigures.name: Cerinthus
keyFigures.role: He is not mentioned in 2 John. He is sometimes suggested as an example of the sort of teaching John’s writings opposed, but the letter does not name any opponent, and the link is a scholarly proposal.

keyThemes.explanation:
The elder loves ‘in truth,’ speaks of the truth that abides in believers, and ends his greeting with ‘in truth and love.’ He asks them to love one another and warns against false teaching.

The letter presents loving others and holding to the truth as two parts of one faithful life.

‘This is love, that we walk according to his commandments.’ The command to love is the one they had ‘from the beginning.’

The text links love and obedience closely, in line with John 14:15 and 1 John 5:3.

keyThemes.theme: Guarding the true teaching about Christ
keyThemes.explanation:
Deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are a danger. Whoever ‘goes on ahead’ and ‘does not abide in the teaching of Christ’ ‘does not have God.’

The letter calls readers to stay anchored to the apostolic teaching about who Jesus is.

Readers are told not to receive or greet someone who does not bring the teaching, because greeting such a person shares in his wicked works.

The text asks readers to consider what they are supporting when they offer help and welcome. It does not give a general rule for every kind of disagreement.

keyThemes.theme: Perseverance and complete joy in fellowship
keyThemes.explanation:
The readers are urged to watch themselves so as not to lose what has been worked for, and the elder hopes to visit so that ‘our joy may be complete.’

The letter encourages watchfulness and sees personal fellowship as a source of joy.
